title: Act V, Scene VI

teacherSummary.text: Before Dunsinane, Malcolm orders the soldiers to throw down their 'leavy screens' and show themselves as they are. His uncle Siward and Siward's son will lead the first battle; Malcolm and Macduff will do the rest. Macduff calls for all the trumpets to sound, 'those clamorous harbingers of blood and death.'

context.history: Short battle scenes with alarums (trumpet calls) and quick exits created the impression of a large battle on a bare stage.

significance: The disguise is dropped as the play moves from concealment to open conflict, matching its theme of appearances giving way to reality.
discussionQuestions: Why do you think the play moves so quickly from scene to scene at the end?
Where does setting appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with fate and free will?

writingPrompts.label: Scaffolded support
writingPrompts.text: Supported track (work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Act V, Scene VI,” how does Shakespeare show the army reveals itself? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the setting you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Act V, Scene VI, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of the army reveals itself? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the setting in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act V, Scene VI develops the idea of the army reveals itself. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of setting and imagery shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act V, Scene VI (where it begins, turns and ends) and its setting shape the reader's understanding of the army reveals itself. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act V, Scene VI suggests about the army reveals itself. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's setting and imagery), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses setting in Act V, Scene VI to complicate the reader's understanding of the army reveals itself. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act V, Scene VI within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of the army reveals itself responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act V, Scene VI alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of the army reveals itself follows or bends those conventions, using the setting as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act V, Scene VI and its treatment of the army reveals itself. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's setting and imagery, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act V, Scene VI as evidence for a larger claim about the army reveals itself in Macbeth. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act V, Scene VI as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of the army reveals itself. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Macbeth.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
